newsitem.title: UK: British disarm 50 kg bomb near Sinn Fein office.
newsitem.headline: British disarm 50 kg bomb near Sinn Fein office.

text.p: The British army defused a bomb packed with 50 kg (110 pounds) of explosives planted on Monday outside an office used by Sinn Fein, the political arm of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
Sinn Fein said it believed the bomb -- a car carrying 50 kilos of home-made explosives packed into beer keg -- was planted by pro-British "Loyalists".
The foiled attack coincided with an election campaign visit by Prime Minister John Major.

Police said homes on the Falls Road, a stronghold of Northern Ireland's minority Catholics, would have been damaged if the bomb had exploded. British army technical experts disarmed it after a warning was telephoned to a radio station.
Senior Sinn Fein official Gerry Kelly said in a statement: "This bomb attack was carried out by Loyalists" and was the fifth such incident at Sinn Fein premises in recent months."

Protestant Loyalists, who want Northern Ireland to remain British, say they are operating a truce, but their foot soldiers have been widely blamed for shooting dead one Catholic and injuring others, in apparent revenge attacks for IRA actions. The IRA abandoned its own cease-fire in February 1996.
In a separate incident in the troubled province, a prison officer was taken hostage at Maghabery jail north of Belfast but released after several hours, the prison service said.

The incident happened in part of the prison that holds inmates linked to a left-wing republican guerrilla group, the Irish National Liberation Army. The prison service said the officer had been seized by two inmates armed with an unspecified weapon.
"The situation ended peacefully. The prisoners have given up their weapon voluntarily. They have been searched and taken to the segregation unit," a spokeswoman told Reuters.
